note_on_method: These notes are researched, not visited. Nobody working on this directory has played on a Seattle court, and none of the writing below pretends otherwise: there is no crowding, no surface condition, no sense of the place on a Saturday morning, because no source states any of that and inventing it would be the most damaging thing this site could ship. Each note contains what Seattle Parks records about that site, where it sits among the twenty-four verified venues, and what the imported commercial record claimed where the city says otherwise.

slots.description:
Green Lake Park East is the largest pickleball site Seattle Parks records, with eight courts striped for tennis and pickleball on the east side of the lake, and it is the only one in the city running an organised open-play programme. That programme is what makes it different from every other entry in this directory. Since 1 October 2025 the city has staffed scheduled sessions here with ambassadors who arrange games and run a paddle stacking system, a rotation queue that calls you into the next game rather than needing you to arrive as a group of four. It was set up as a one-year pilot, so its future beyond autumn 2026 is not known.

The imported commercial record listed Green Lake as four courts, two of them indoor. Seattle Parks records eight courts, all outdoor.
slots.getting_there: Seattle Parks records dedicated parking at this site and gives the address as 7201 E Green Lake Dr N. The lot belongs to Green Lake Park as a whole, and the park draws walkers, runners and rowers all day, so a dedicated lot existing is not the same as a space being free when you arrive. The city publishes no capacity or time-limit information for it, so read the posted signs. An all-year restroom is recorded on site.
slots.what_to_expect: Eight courts with nets provided, no lights, and tennis lines under your feet. If you are coming alone or as a pair, come inside one of the open-play windows (Monday 8 to 10 a.m., Wednesday 1 to 3 p.m., Saturday 9 to 11 a.m., or Sunday 4 to 6 p.m.), because that is when the rotation runs. Outside those hours it is first come, first served. With no lighting recorded, play ends when the light does.

faqs.q: Can I turn up alone and get a game?
faqs.a: Yes, during the open-play windows. Ambassadors run a paddle stacking system in those sessions so single players rotate in. Outside those hours you are on your own like anywhere else.
No. All eight are outdoor, and there is no covered or climate-controlled pickleball recorded anywhere in Seattle.
Not verified. Seattle Parks publishes no fee information for its pickleball courts, so cost shows as unverified rather than assumed free.

slots.description: Gilman Playground in Ballard carries four courts striped for tennis and pickleball, and it is one of three Seattle sites where the city has formally restricted when you may play. In September 2025 Seattle Parks, working with the Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections, ran noise studies at this location and found play producing sound levels above the limits set in Seattle Municipal Code chapter 25.08. The result was a posted schedule with real enforcement behind it, which shapes both when the courts are open and how the neighbours are likely to feel about a loud evening game.
slots.getting_there: The address Seattle Parks records is 923 NW 54th St, and the city records street parking rather than a dedicated lot. This is a residential Ballard block, and no capacity, permit or time-limit information is published for it, so read the posted signs. A seasonal restroom is recorded, so do not count on it out of season.
slots.what_to_expect: Four courts, nets provided, and no lights recorded, which matters here because the posted hours run to 10 p.m. and nothing illuminates the court after dusk. Play is permitted 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. at weekends and city-observed holidays, in force since 15 September 2025. Those hours are enforced: a violation captured on timestamped photo or video results in a lock fitted to the courts for at least thirty days, and repeat violations make the lock permanent, after which the courts open only when staff are on site to unlock them.

faqs.q: What time do the courts close?
faqs.a: 10 p.m. every day, with opening at 7 a.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m. at weekends and city-observed holidays. These hours took effect on 15 September 2025.
Yes. Seattle Parks records nets at this location. The city records nets at seventeen of its twenty-five pickleball sites and says nothing either way about the other eight.

slots.description:
Laurelhurst Playfield holds a single dedicated pickleball court, one of only three dedicated pickleball sites among the twenty-four verified Seattle venues; every other site is striped over tennis or shared with basketball or badminton. Being dedicated is the good news and being one court is the bad news, and the second is the more useful fact when deciding whether to drive here. It is also one of three Seattle locations where the city imposed restricted hours in September 2025 after noise studies with the Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections found play exceeding the limits in Seattle Municipal Code chapter 25.08.

The imported record placed this venue at 4339 NE 43rd St. The city's own parcel record puts it at 4544 NE 41st St, two blocks away, and that is the address published here.
slots.getting_there: Seattle Parks records the address as 4544 NE 41st St; the imported record had this venue two blocks away on NE 43rd St. Dedicated parking is recorded on site, along with an all-year restroom. The city publishes no capacity or restriction detail for the parking, and it has not been checked in person.
slots.what_to_expect: One court, nets provided, no lights. A single court means one game at a time, so on a good weekend afternoon expect either a wait or a rotation negotiated between whoever is there. Play is permitted 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. at weekends and city-observed holidays, and those hours carry the same enforcement as the other two restricted sites: timestamped evidence of play outside them leads to a lock for a minimum of thirty days, permanent on repeat.

faqs.q: Is this a dedicated pickleball court?
faqs.a: Yes, and that is rare here. Seattle Parks records only four dedicated pickleball locations in the city and three of them, including this one, have a single court. Every other verified Seattle venue shares its surface with tennis, basketball or badminton.

faqs.q: Are nets provided, and is there a restroom?
faqs.a: Nets yes, and an all-year restroom is recorded on site. Eleven of the twenty-five Seattle pickleball locations have only a seasonal restroom and three have none recorded at all.

slots.description: Mt. Baker Park carries four courts striped for tennis and pickleball, and it is the only one of the three restricted-hours sites that also has lights. The city recorded lighting here, and then in September 2025 capped play at 10 p.m. after noise studies with the Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections found sound levels above the limits in Seattle Municipal Code chapter 25.08. So the lights exist and the clock still stops. Of the five lit venues among the twenty-four verified Seattle sites, this is the one where the lights are least useful late.
slots.getting_there: The address Seattle Parks records is 2521 Lake Park Dr S; the imported record had the street with no number, and the city's parcel record supplied it. Street parking rather than a dedicated lot, on a residential block above Lake Washington, with an all-year restroom recorded on site. No permit or time-limit information is published, so read the posted signs.
slots.what_to_expect: Four courts with nets provided and lights, open 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. at weekends and city-observed holidays. Enforcement is the same as at Gilman and Laurelhurst: play documented outside posted hours with timestamped visual evidence results in a lock for at least thirty days, and further violations make it permanent. The trigger is documented evidence rather than a complaint, so the posted hours are worth taking literally. If you want lit courts without a curfew, Bitter Lake Playfield and Rainier Beach Playfield are the two larger lit sites with no restricted-hours order recorded against them.

faqs.q: It has lights. Can I play late?
faqs.a: Until 10 p.m. and no later. This is the only Seattle venue that is both lit and curfewed, so the lights are useful on winter afternoons and capped at night.
Street parking; Seattle Parks records no dedicated lot here. No permit or time-limit information is published, so read the posted signs.

slots.description:
Bitter Lake Playfield holds eight courts striped for tennis and pickleball under lights, which makes it one of exactly two sites in Seattle offering both the largest court count and evening play. Between it and Rainier Beach Playfield sit sixteen of the ninety-two verified courts in the city.

The imported commercial dataset held two separate Bitter Lake entries: a community centre with three indoor courts, and a second row claiming eleven courts of which three were indoor. Seattle Parks records one pickleball site at this address, with eight courts, all outdoor. This page is the outdoor playfield; the community centre is a separate building with its own indoor courts and is not published here.
slots.getting_there: Seattle Parks records the address as 13035 Linden Ave N and gives this site dedicated parking rather than street parking. The restroom is recorded as seasonal, so it is not something to count on outside the warm months. No capacity, permit or time-limit information is published for the parking.
slots.what_to_expect: Eight courts, nets provided, and lights: the fullest combination available in Seattle on the city's own record. The courts are shared with tennis, so expect tennis lines underfoot and the possibility of a booked court. There is no posted-hours order against this location in the records checked, unlike Gilman, Laurelhurst and Mt. Baker, so the lights are not capped by a curfew. What Seattle Parks does not publish is when the lights actually run or whether they are switched on seasonally, so treat evening play as possible rather than guaranteed. No crowding or peak-time data is published for any venue.

faqs.q: Is this the same place as Bitter Lake Community Center?
faqs.a: No. The community centre is a building with three indoor courts of its own; this record is the outdoor playfield with eight. They share a campus.

faqs.q: How does it compare with Rainier Beach?
faqs.a: They are the two eight-court lit sites in Seattle. Rainier Beach has an all-year restroom where Bitter Lake's is seasonal; both have dedicated parking and nets. On the city's record the two are close to interchangeable.

slots.description: Rainier Beach Playfield carries eight lit courts striped for tennis and pickleball, tying it with Bitter Lake for the largest lit site in the verified Seattle set. It is also the one venue where the imported record and the city agreed exactly on the court count: eight outdoor courts in both. The same import also held a Rainier Beach Community Center row claiming three indoor courts. That is a different venue, a building with its own courts, and it is not published here.
slots.getting_there: Seattle Parks gives the address as 4707 S Cloverdale St and records dedicated parking and an all-year restroom, the better of the two restroom categories the city uses. Eleven of the twenty-five sites in the dataset have an all-year restroom, eleven are seasonal, and three have none recorded. No permit or time-limit detail is published for the parking.
slots.what_to_expect: Eight courts with nets provided and lights, shared with tennis. No restricted-hours order is recorded against this site, so unlike Mt. Baker the lights are not paired with a 10 p.m. curfew. Combined with dedicated parking and an all-year restroom, this is one of the better-equipped venues in the city on the record, though nothing is published about how busy any court gets. The gaps are the standard Seattle ones: no surface type, no fee and no published hours for the site, and nothing about the hours the lights operate.

faqs.a: No. Seattle Parks records the playfield and the community centre separately, and this page is the playfield: eight outdoor courts. The community centre's three indoor courts have not been verified, so they do not appear on this site.

faqs.q: How does it compare with Bitter Lake?
faqs.a: They are the only two eight-court lit venues in the city and are near-identical on the record: nets, dedicated parking, lights, tennis-shared. The one difference Seattle Parks records is the restroom, all-year here and seasonal at Bitter Lake. Neither carries a posted-hours order.

slots.description: West Magnolia Playfield has eight courts striped for tennis and pickleball, dedicated parking and an all-year restroom: a substantial site by any reading, and one the imported commercial directory had no row for at all. It is listed here from Seattle Parks' own pickleball dataset. It is the largest unlit site in Seattle, sharing the eight-court tier with Bitter Lake, Rainier Beach and Green Lake East but without their evening option. It is not the same place as Magnolia Community Center, a nearby indoor building with three courts of its own.
slots.getting_there: The Parks record gives 2518 34th Ave W, with dedicated parking and an all-year restroom. Every fact on this page, including the address, comes from the city. No capacity or restriction information is published for the parking and none has been checked in person.
slots.what_to_expect: Eight courts, nets provided, no lights recorded. That makes it the largest daylight-only site in the city: plenty of capacity, and nothing to extend it past dusk, which in a Seattle December means play ends before half past four. Shared with tennis, like most Seattle courts. No crowding data is published, so whether eight courts is enough on a Saturday is not known. The other gaps are the city's gaps: no surface type, no fee and no hours.

faqs.a: No. The community centre is an indoor building nearby with three courts, recorded separately, and it has not been verified against a named source.
No. Seattle Parks records no lighting here, and unlike a venue where the city is simply silent, this is a positive record of absence.

faqs.q: Is eight courts a lot for Seattle?
faqs.a: It is the joint maximum. Four sites in the city have eight courts and nothing has more: this one, Bitter Lake, Rainier Beach and Green Lake East. Of those four, two are lit and two are not, and West Magnolia is in the unlit half.

slots.description: Miller Playfield on Capitol Hill carries five courts under lights, which makes it the largest lit site in the centre of the city. Seattle Parks names the parcel Pendleton Miller Playfield. The imported record claimed four courts; the city says five. The same import held a separate Miller Community Center row at the same 330 19th Ave E address, claiming seven courts of which three were indoor. That is the building beside the playfield, not these courts, and the two are kept separate here.
slots.getting_there: The address is 330 19th Ave E, which the import and the city agreed on. Dedicated parking and an all-year restroom are both recorded. The playfield sits inside a dense residential grid, and while the city records a dedicated lot it publishes nothing about its size or its restrictions.
slots.what_to_expect: Five courts, nets provided, lights, shared with tennis. No restricted-hours order applies here in the records checked, so the lights are not capped by a curfew the way Mt. Baker's are. For anyone in the centre of Seattle this is the only lit option that is not a substantial drive. No peak-time or crowding information is published, and the remaining gaps are the ones Seattle carries everywhere: no surface type, no fee and no published hours for this site.

faqs.q: Is this the same as Miller Community Center?
faqs.a: No, though they share an address. The community centre is the indoor building; this is the outdoor playfield with five courts.

faqs.q: How many courts are there, really?
faqs.a: Five. The imported record said four. Seattle Parks, which operates the site, records five, and a city record wins on a fact about its own facility.

faqs.q: Why is it called Pendleton Miller Playfield on some maps?
faqs.a: That is the name on the city's parcel record. The pickleball dataset calls the same site Miller Playfield, and that shorter form is used here.

slots.description: Delridge Playfield holds four courts striped for tennis and pickleball in West Seattle. The imported dataset claimed seven courts here, three of them indoor. Seattle Parks records four courts, all outdoor, and there is no verified indoor pickleball at this site or anywhere else in the city. The address was wrong as well, by roughly a block on the same street. This page is built from the city record. It is kept separate from the Delridge Community Center row, which is the indoor building nearby.
slots.getting_there: Seattle Parks gives 4458 Delridge Way SW; the imported record had 4501, about a block north. Dedicated parking is recorded, along with a seasonal restroom, which means present in the warm months and not something to plan around in February. No parking restrictions have been checked on the ground.
slots.what_to_expect: Four courts, nets provided, no lights. Shared with tennis, so expect tennis lines and the possibility of a booked court. With no lighting recorded, play here is bounded by daylight, and Seattle daylight in midwinter ends before half past four. What the city does not record is a long list on this venue: no surface type, no resurfacing history, no fee, no opening hours, and nothing about whether four courts is enough on a Saturday.

faqs.q: Are there indoor courts at Delridge?
faqs.a: Not at this venue. The imported record claimed three and the city records none. There is a Delridge Community Center nearby which is an indoor building, but it has not been verified against a named source, so it does not appear on this site.

faqs.q: Is there anywhere lit nearby in West Seattle?
faqs.a: Alki Playground is the lit option in West Seattle, with four courts and street parking. Walt Hundley Playfield is also close and also unlit. Only five of the twenty-four verified Seattle venues have lighting recorded at all.

slots.description: Alki Playground carries four lit courts striped for tennis and pickleball, one of only five lit venues among the twenty-four verified in Seattle. It sits in West Seattle above the Alki shoreline. The court count and the address both matched the city record exactly. The imported record typed this venue as a dedicated pickleball facility; Seattle Parks records it as a park whose courts are shared between tennis and pickleball, which is a materially different thing to arrive at with a paddle and an expectation. The city's typing is the one published here.
slots.getting_there: The address is 5817 SW Lander St. Seattle Parks records street parking rather than a dedicated lot, and a seasonal restroom. The city publishes no capacity or restriction data for the parking, so read the posted signs rather than trusting an assumption about a shoreline destination.
slots.what_to_expect: Four courts, nets provided, lights, shared with tennis. No posted-hours order is recorded against this site. Among the five lit Seattle venues this is the only one with street rather than dedicated parking, which is the practical trade-off to weigh against Bitter Lake or Rainier Beach if you are driving to an evening game. The city publishes no surface type, no fee, no hours, no lighting hours, and nothing about how the courts fill on a summer weekend at a beachfront park.

faqs.q: Is this a dedicated pickleball facility?
faqs.a: No, despite what some listings say. Seattle Parks records a shared tennis and pickleball surface. Expect tennis lines and shared use.

faqs.q: Is it the best lit option in West Seattle?
faqs.a: It is the only one. Delridge and Walt Hundley, the other two verified West Seattle sites, both have no lighting recorded. The trade-off is parking, which is street here rather than the dedicated lots at Bitter Lake and Rainier Beach.

slots.description: Beacon Hill Park holds four courts striped for tennis and pickleball. The city's own data disagrees with itself on the name: Seattle Parks calls the parcel BEACON HILL PLAYGROUND in its property record while the pickleball layer calls the same site Beacon Hill Park. Both describe the same courts at the same address. The pickleball layer's name is published here because that is the record describing these courts specifically. The imported record offered a third variation, Beacon Hill Playground Tennis Courts.
slots.getting_there: The address is 1902 13th Ave S, which the import and both city records agree on. Seattle Parks records street parking and a seasonal restroom. The courts sit inside a dense residential neighbourhood; the city publishes no parking capacity or restriction detail, so read the signs.
slots.what_to_expect: Four courts, nets provided, no lights recorded, shared with tennis. With no lighting this is a daylight venue, which for a large part of the Seattle year makes it a lunchtime and weekend court rather than an after-work one. Seattle Parks records no surface type, no fee and no hours for this site, and nothing about how busy four shared courts get on a weekday evening in a dense neighbourhood.

faqs.a: No. Seattle Parks positively records no lighting at this site, which is a different statement from the city simply being silent about it.

faqs.q: Is the restroom open all year?
faqs.a: No, the city records it as seasonal. Eleven of the twenty-five Seattle sites have seasonal restrooms, eleven are all-year and three have none recorded.

faqs.q: What is nearby if this is busy?
faqs.a: Dearborn Park is the closest other verified venue, also four courts and also unlit, though it has no restroom recorded. The nearest lit courts are at Mt. Baker Park, which carries a 10 p.m. curfew imposed by the city after noise studies.

slots.description: Brighton Playfield carries four courts striped for tennis and pickleball in south Seattle. Almost nothing needed correcting here: the name, the address and the court count all came through the import intact and the city record confirmed each one. That is unusual in the Seattle set, and the practical consequence for a reader is that everything on this page was confirmed rather than repaired.
slots.getting_there: Seattle Parks gives 6000 39th Ave S, matching the imported address exactly. The city records street parking and an all-year restroom, the better of the two restroom categories it uses. No parking capacity, permit or time-limit information is published and none has been verified on the ground.
slots.what_to_expect: Four courts, nets provided, no lights recorded, shared with tennis. An all-year restroom and four courts make this a reasonable daylight option in south Seattle; the absence of lighting is the constraint, and it is a positively recorded absence rather than an unknown. There is no surface record, no fee record and no hours record for Brighton, and nothing is published about how the four courts fill.

faqs.a: Yes, and the city records it as all-year rather than seasonal. That puts it among the eleven Seattle pickleball sites with a year-round restroom.

faqs.q: Can I play in the evening?
faqs.a: Not under lights. Seattle Parks records no lighting here, so play is bounded by daylight.

faqs.q: What else is verified in south Seattle?
faqs.a: Rainier Beach Playfield is the substantial one, with eight lit courts, dedicated parking and an all-year restroom. Lakeridge Park is further south with two badminton-shared courts. Brighton sits between them in size at four courts, and unlike Rainier Beach it has no lighting recorded.

faqs.q: Is the court count reliable here?
faqs.a: Four courts is what Seattle Parks records and what the imported data said. Where the operator and an independent record agree on a fact about the operator's own facility, that is about as good as verification gets short of standing on the court.

slots.description: Dearborn Park holds four courts striped for tennis and pickleball, and it is the clearest case in the Seattle set of an imported record understating a venue. The commercial dataset claimed two courts. Seattle Parks records four. Dearborn is also one of only three verified Seattle venues where the city records no nearby restroom at all, which is a practical detail worth more than most of the fields on this page.
slots.getting_there: The address is 2919 S Brandon St, agreed between the import and the city. Seattle Parks records street parking, and records the restroom as absent rather than seasonal, which is a positive statement that there is none. No parking capacity or restriction information is published.
slots.what_to_expect: Four courts, no lights recorded, shared with tennis, and the city does not state whether nets are provided here, so that field shows as unverified rather than as a no. Combined with no restroom on site, this is a venue to arrive at prepared. Beyond that the usual absences apply: no surface type, no fee, no hours, and nothing about how four courts hold up under demand.

faqs.a: Four, per Seattle Parks. The imported record said two, so this is one of the few Seattle venues where the unverified data undercounted rather than overcounted.
No. The city records no nearby restroom at this site, a positive record of absence rather than a gap in the data. Only three of the twenty-five Seattle locations are recorded this way.
Unknown. Seattle Parks records nets at seventeen of its twenty-five pickleball locations and says nothing either way about the other eight, of which this is one. Bring a portable net if you have one.

slots.description: Discovery Park is the largest park in Seattle, and the four courts recorded inside it are striped for tennis and pickleball. The imported commercial record carried the name as Discovery Park? Tennis and Pickleball Courts, with an encoding artefact where a character failed to survive a file conversion. The venue name here is taken from the city record instead, which is both correct and shorter. The court count and address matched the city record.
slots.getting_there: Seattle Parks gives the address as 3801 Discovery Park Blvd and records dedicated parking with an all-year restroom. Discovery Park is large and its parking serves the whole park rather than the courts, so a dedicated lot existing is not the same as a space being free near the courts when you get there. The city publishes no capacity detail, and nothing about how far the lot is from the courts.
slots.what_to_expect: Four courts, no lights recorded, shared with tennis. Nets are not recorded either way by the city, so that field shows as unverified rather than as an absence. Being inside a large park with an all-year restroom and a dedicated lot puts the practical basics in place; what is missing is any lighting, which bounds play to daylight. The city also records no surface type, no fee and no hours, and no crowding data is published.

faqs.a: The city does not say. Seattle Parks records nets at seventeen of twenty-five locations and is silent about eight, including this one, so the page shows nets as unverified rather than guessing in either direction.
Not known. The city records a dedicated lot, but Discovery Park is the largest park in Seattle and that lot serves all of it. No capacity or restriction data is published.

faqs.q: Is it worth the trip for four courts?
faqs.a: The record supports this much: four shared courts, no lights, an all-year restroom and a dedicated lot, inside the largest park in the city. Four courts is the median size in the verified Seattle set, so this is a typical site in an atypical setting.

slots.description: Georgetown Playfield carries four courts striped for tennis and pickleball in the industrial south of the city. Like Discovery Park and Soundview, its imported name arrived damaged, as Georgetown ?Playfield Tennis and Pickleball Courts, with an encoding artefact in the middle of it. The court count and address both matched the city record, and the name published above comes from Seattle Parks.
slots.getting_there: Seattle Parks gives 750 S Homer St, matching the import exactly. The city records street parking and an all-year restroom. Georgetown is a mixed industrial and residential neighbourhood, and the city publishes no capacity or restriction data for parking there, so read the posted signs.
slots.what_to_expect: Four courts, no lights recorded, shared with tennis. The city does not state whether nets are provided at this site, so that field reads as unverified rather than as an absence. An all-year restroom is recorded, which puts it among the better-served eleven of twenty-five on that one measure. The city does not record a surface type, does not publish a fee and does not publish hours. What it does record is the court count, the outdoor split, the absence of lighting, street parking and the restroom. That is enough to decide whether to travel and not enough to describe the experience of playing here.

faqs.a: The city does not say. Seattle Parks records nets at seventeen of its twenty-five pickleball locations and is silent about eight, and Georgetown is one of the eight. Silence is not a no, so the page says unverified.
No. The city positively records no lighting here, so play is bounded by daylight.

faqs.q: Should I expect to share the courts?
faqs.a: Almost certainly. This is a tennis and pickleball surface, which describes eighteen of the twenty-five Seattle locations the city records. How often it is actually contested is not known, because Seattle Parks publishes no booking or usage data for any of its courts.

slots.description: Soundview Playfield holds four courts striped for tennis and pickleball in Crown Hill, in the north-west of the city. Its imported name arrived as Soundview ?Playfield Tennis and Pickleball Courts (Crown Hill), carrying both an encoding artefact and a neighbourhood in brackets, so the name published here is the city's. The underlying facts came through accurately: four courts, and an address that matched. Fields the city does not record, including whether nets are provided, read as unverified.
slots.getting_there: Seattle Parks gives 1590 NW 90th St, matching the imported address exactly. The city records street parking and a seasonal restroom, meaning present in the warm months and not something to depend on in winter. No capacity or restriction detail is published for the parking.
slots.what_to_expect: Four courts, no lights recorded, shared with tennis, and nets unrecorded either way. In a city where nineteen of twenty-four verified venues have no lighting, the daylight constraint here is the norm rather than a mark against the venue, but it is worth planning around between October and March. There is no surface record, no fee and no published hours, and nothing about how four shared courts in Crown Hill fill through the week. Four courts is the median size in the verified Seattle set.

faqs.a: Unknown. Seattle Parks does not record nets at this location, and an absent record is treated as unknown rather than as a no. A portable net is cheap insurance.
No, the city records this one as seasonal.

faqs.q: What else is verified in north-west Seattle?
faqs.a: Gilman Playground in Ballard has four courts and carries a city-imposed 10 p.m. curfew after noise studies; Bitter Lake Playfield further north has eight courts under lights. Soundview sits between them in size with four unlit courts and no posted-hours order recorded against it.

slots.description: Walt Hundley Playfield carries four courts striped for tennis and pickleball in West Seattle, and it is one of the venues the imported commercial dataset had no row for at all. The playfield shares its address, 6920 34th Ave SW, with High Point Community Center, and the import did hold a row for the community centre claiming three indoor courts. They are two facilities: a building with its own courts, and an outdoor playfield with four. The playfield is published from the city record; the community centre remains unverified.
slots.getting_there: The address Seattle Parks records is 6920 34th Ave SW, the same address as the community centre next to it, which is worth knowing if you are navigating by postcode. Dedicated parking is recorded, along with a seasonal restroom. The city publishes no capacity or restriction information for the parking.
slots.what_to_expect: Four courts, nets provided, no lights recorded, shared with tennis. Every fact above came from the city and none from a commercial record. What the city does not publish, including surface, fees, hours and how busy it gets, is shown as unverified. What it does publish is the court count, the outdoor split, the absence of lighting, nets, dedicated parking and a seasonal restroom.

faqs.q: Is this High Point Community Center?
faqs.a: No, though they share an address. The community centre is an indoor building with its own courts; this is the outdoor playfield with four.
Yes. Seattle Parks records nets at this location, as it does at seventeen of its twenty-five pickleball sites.
No. Seattle Parks records no lighting here, so play is bounded by daylight, and the nearest lit courts in West Seattle are at Alki Playground.

slots.description: Lakeridge Park holds two courts in the far south of Seattle, and it is the only verified venue in the city whose courts are shared with badminton rather than tennis or basketball. Of twenty-five locations Seattle Parks records, eighteen share with tennis, two with basketball, one with badminton, and four are dedicated. Lakeridge is the one. The imported row carried a postal code of 10145, which is not a postcode at all: it is the street number from 10145 Rainier Ave S, leaked into the wrong column. It is not published anywhere on this site.
slots.getting_there: Seattle Parks gives 10145 Rainier Ave S and records dedicated parking with a seasonal restroom. No parking capacity or restriction data is published for the site and none has been checked on the ground.
slots.what_to_expect: Two courts, nets provided, no lights, shared with badminton. Two courts is a small site, and being shared with a sport that uses a different net height and court marking is worth knowing before you drive to the south end of the city for it. Nets are recorded as provided, which on a badminton-shared court is a more useful fact than usual, though the city's record does not say which sport's net is set up. Seattle Parks publishes no surface type, no fee, no hours and no information about how busy the courts get.

faqs.q: Is this really a badminton court?
faqs.a: It is recorded by Seattle Parks as shared badminton and pickleball use, and it is the only site in the city recorded that way. Expect markings for both.
Two, per the city record, with nets provided.

faqs.q: What else is nearby in south Seattle?
faqs.a: Rainier Beach Playfield is the substantial option, with eight lit courts, dedicated parking and an all-year restroom. Brighton Playfield has four unlit courts. Against those, Lakeridge is small and unusual rather than convenient.

slots.description: Observatory Courts sits on Queen Anne with two courts striped for tennis and pickleball. The imported record claimed four. Seattle Parks records two, so the commercial data doubled the capacity of the site, and on a two-court venue that is the difference between turning up expecting to wait and turning up expecting not to. Observatory is also one of only three verified Seattle venues where the city records no nearby restroom.
slots.getting_there: Seattle Parks gives 1405 Warren Ave N, which the imported record matched. The city records street parking, on a dense residential part of Queen Anne, and no restroom. No capacity, permit or time-limit detail is published for the parking, so read the signs.
slots.what_to_expect: Two courts, no lights, shared with tennis, and nets not recorded either way by the city. With no restroom and no lighting recorded, this is a daylight venue to arrive at prepared. The city does not record whether nets are provided, what the surface is, what it costs, when it is open, or how two courts on Queen Anne cope with a summer evening. Two shared courts puts this in the smallest third of Seattle venues, and eight sites in the verified set are smaller still.

faqs.a: Two. The imported record said four. On a site this size that is a doubling.
No. The city records none at this site, one of only three Seattle pickleball locations recorded that way.
Unknown. Seattle Parks does not record nets here, and an absent record is not treated as a no.

faqs.q: What is the other Queen Anne option?
faqs.a: Kinnear Park, which has one shared court and a seasonal restroom. Between the two sites Queen Anne has three shared courts and no lighting recorded at either.

slots.description: Maple Leaf Reservoir Park holds two courts, and they are dedicated pickleball courts rather than tennis courts with extra lines on them. Of the twenty-five locations Seattle Parks records, only four are dedicated, and this is the largest of them, the other three being single courts. It is also one of the four venues the imported dataset had no row for at all. Every fact on this page came from the city.
slots.getting_there: Seattle Parks gives 1020 NE 82nd St and records street parking with an all-year restroom. An all-year restroom puts it among the better-served eleven of the twenty-five sites on that measure. No parking capacity or restriction information is published.
slots.what_to_expect: Two courts, nets provided, no lights, and no tennis lines to share the surface with. For a two-court site that combination is unusually clean: dedicated markings, nets on site, and a restroom that works in February. What it does not have is lighting, so play is bounded by daylight, and it does not have the capacity of the eight-court playfields. The gaps are the same as elsewhere: no surface record, no fee, no hours, and nothing about how busy it gets.

faqs.a: Yes. Seattle Parks records the use type here as pickleball rather than shared, which applies to only four of the twenty-five locations in the city dataset.
Yes, and the city records it as all-year rather than seasonal.

faqs.q: How does it compare with the other dedicated courts?
faqs.a: There are four dedicated pickleball sites in the city and this is the only one with two courts; South Park Playground and Laurelhurst Playfield have one each, and the fourth is an SDOT street-end court not published for want of a sourced address. So on the city's record this is the largest dedicated pickleball venue in Seattle, which says more about the city's provision than about the site.

slots.description: Kinnear Park on Queen Anne holds a single court shared with tennis. The imported record claimed three, so the commercial data tripled a one-court venue, the largest proportional court-count error anywhere in the Seattle set. Kinnear is also the one Seattle case where the city record itself needed correcting: the Parks record gives the street as 899 W Olumpic Pl, a misspelling of Olympic Place in the municipal data. The spelling is corrected here and the original wording is preserved in the evidence behind the address.
slots.getting_there: The address is 899 W Olympic Pl, corrected from the city's own record as described above. Seattle Parks records street parking and a seasonal restroom. Queen Anne is dense and residential; the city publishes nothing about parking capacity, permits or time limits.
slots.what_to_expect: One court, no lights, shared with tennis, and nets not recorded either way. A single shared court is the smallest unit of provision in this directory, and there are seven other Seattle venues in the same position. It means one game at a time and whatever rotation the people present agree on. The city does not record whether nets are provided here, does not publish a surface type, a fee or any hours, and publishes nothing about demand. So there is one shared court at a corrected address on Queen Anne, and whether you will get on it is not known.

faqs.a: One. The imported record said three. On a single-court site that changes whether a trip is worth making.
It is now. The city's own record misspells the street as Olumpic Place; the corrected spelling is published here and the original is kept in the evidence attached to the address.

faqs.q: Is one court worth the trip?
faqs.a: That depends on where you are starting from and who else turns up. Observatory Courts is the other Queen Anne site, with two shared courts and no restroom recorded, so the immediate area offers three shared courts in total across two venues. Neither is lit.

slots.description: Montlake Playfield holds a single court, and it is one of only two verified Seattle venues where the pickleball surface is shared with basketball rather than tennis. That matters more than the usual tennis sharing does: a tennis court with pickleball lines is at least a racquet-sport surface with a net post in roughly the right place, whereas a basketball court with pickleball markings is a different proposition, and the city records nothing about how nets are handled on it. The court count and address both matched the imported record.
slots.getting_there: Seattle Parks gives 1618 E Calhoun St and records dedicated parking with a seasonal restroom. Dedicated parking on a single-court site is unusual in this set; it reflects the parking serving the whole playfield rather than the court. No capacity or restriction detail is published.
slots.what_to_expect: One court, no lights, shared with basketball, and nets not recorded either way by the city. Given the shared use and the silence on nets, this is a venue to bring a portable net to unless you have been before and know otherwise. One court means one game. The city also publishes no surface type, no fee, no hours and nothing about demand. A basketball surface with pickleball lines and no net is not a pickleball court in any useful sense, and which of those you would find is not known.

faqs.q: Is this a proper pickleball court?
faqs.a: It is a shared-use court recorded by Seattle Parks as basketball and pickleball. Only two Seattle venues are recorded that way. Expect basketball markings and pickleball lines on the same surface.
Unknown. The city does not record nets here, and on a basketball-shared surface that is a question worth resolving before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there a better option nearby?
faqs.a: Miller Playfield is the closest substantial venue, with five courts under lights on Capitol Hill, on a tennis-shared surface with nets recorded. Montlake offers one court whose net provision the city does not state.

slots.description: South Park Playground holds a single dedicated pickleball court, one of only four dedicated sites in the city and one of three that consist of exactly one court. It is also the venue with the largest address disagreement in the Seattle set. The imported record placed it at 8319 8th Ave S. Seattle Parks places its own parcel at 738 S Sullivan St, a different street. The municipal address is published here, because the city is describing property it owns.
slots.getting_there: The address is 738 S Sullivan St, corrected from the imported 8319 8th Ave S. Seattle Parks records dedicated parking and an all-year restroom, which for a one-court site is better provision than most. No capacity or restriction detail is published for the parking.
slots.what_to_expect: One court, nets provided, no lights, dedicated to pickleball rather than shared. For a single court that is a good specification: real markings, a net on site, parking and a year-round restroom. The constraint is simply that there is one of it, so a busy afternoon is a queue. What the city does not publish is the surface, the cost, the opening hours, and whether one court is enough on any given afternoon. One court puts this among the eight smallest venues in the city, though it is one of only four with dedicated pickleball markings.

faqs.a: 738 S Sullivan St, from the city's parcel record. The imported record had 8319 8th Ave S, which is a different street. A single-court venue is hard enough to find without being sent to the wrong street.

faqs.q: Is this a dedicated pickleball court?
faqs.a: Yes. Seattle Parks records the use type as pickleball rather than shared. Only four of the twenty-five locations in the city dataset are recorded that way.
Yes, the city records nets at this location.

slots.description: Greenwood Park holds a single court shared with basketball. The imported dataset had no row for it, so like Maple Leaf, West Magnolia and Walt Hundley it is listed here from the city's pickleball dataset directly. The city's two records disagree on the spelling: the pickleball layer spells the park Greenwod, dropping a letter, while the Parks property record for the same parcel spells it GREENWOOD PARK. The Parks spelling is published here and the correction recorded, on the same principle as the misspelled street at Kinnear Park.
slots.getting_there: Seattle Parks gives 602 N 87th St and records street parking with a seasonal restroom. The address and every other fact above came from the city. No parking capacity or restriction information is published, so read the posted signs.
slots.what_to_expect: One court, no lights, shared with basketball, and nets not recorded either way. That is the same specification as Montlake Playfield, and the same advice applies: on a basketball-shared surface with no net recorded, a portable net is worth having. One court means one game at a time. The city publishes no surface type, no fee, no hours and nothing about demand. One shared court puts this at the smallest end of the Seattle set, alongside Kinnear Park, Montlake Playfield, Laurelhurst Playfield and South Park Playground.

faqs.a: Greenwood. The city's pickleball dataset spells it Greenwod, dropping a letter; the Parks property record for the same parcel spells it correctly.
Unknown. Seattle Parks does not record nets at this location, and an absent record is not read as a no.

Bitter Lake Playfield is the substantial northern option, with eight courts under lights, nets, dedicated parking and a seasonal restroom. Against that, Greenwood is a single basketball-shared court with no net recorded; the two are not really in the same category.

sources.evidence: Updated racquet court hours at Gilman Playground, Laurelhurst Playfield and Mt. Baker Park effective 15 September 2025: 7:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. weekdays, 9:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. Saturday, Sunday and City-observed holidays. Noise studies with SDCI found levels exceeding Seattle Municipal Code Chapter 25.08. Violations outside posted hours supported with timestamped visual evidence result in temporary lock installation for a minimum of 30 days; subsequent violations trigger permanent locks. Green Lake East open-play pilot from 1 October 2025 for one year: Monday 8-10 a.m., Wednesday 1-3 p.m., Saturday 9-11 a.m., Sunday 4-6 p.m., with ambassadors and a paddle stacking system.
Per-venue court counts, indoor/outdoor, lights, nets, nearby restroom, parking and shared use type.
